title: Every Response Has a Running Time

scenes.visual: Title card 'Every Response Has a Running Time' over a side-view human leg, knee bent, a small reflex hammer near the tendon below the kneecap. COLOUR MAP, same in both films and the lesson: the route is a GOLD line; five stations in fixed order and colours: receptor TEAL, sensory neuron BLUE, integrating centre in the spinal cord GREY, motor neuron ORANGE, effector muscle RED. A horizontal TIMER BAR at the bottom fills one segment per leg in the station colour (sensory BLUE, motor ORANGE), a short WHITE tick for each synapse, and a hatched GREY end block for junction and muscle. Inhibited muscles fade to pale grey. Numbers appear only as on-screen text. Cream background, 16:9. Anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: Tap the tendon below your kneecap, and your leg kicks before you decide anything. How long does that take, and where does the time go?
scenes.visual: The hammer taps the tendon; the lower leg swings forward. A stopwatch icon appears top right with a question mark on its face. The leg settles back and the frame holds.
scenes.narration: Tap the tendon below your kneecap, and your leg kicks before you decide anything. How long does that take, and where does the time go?

scenes.tts: The signal runs a route with five stations. First, a receptor in the thigh muscle detects the stretch. Then a sensory neuron carries the signal up to the spinal cord.
scenes.visual: A GOLD line starts drawing itself from a TEAL dot in the quadriceps (label 'receptor: muscle spindle'), then turns BLUE and runs up the thigh to a GREY cross-section of the spinal cord at the lower back (labels 'sensory neuron', 'spinal cord').
scenes.narration: The signal runs a route with five stations. First, a receptor in the thigh muscle detects the stretch. Then a sensory neuron carries the signal up to the spinal cord.

scenes.tts: In the spinal cord, the integrating centre, it crosses one synapse. A motor neuron carries it back down the leg. Then the effector, the thigh muscle, contracts.
scenes.visual: Inside the GREY cord a WHITE tick flashes where the BLUE line meets an ORANGE line ('1 synapse'). The ORANGE line runs back down to the quadriceps, which glows RED and shortens; the leg kicks. Five labels line up along the top in order: receptor, sensory neuron, integrating centre, motor neuron, effector.
scenes.narration: In the spinal cord, the integrating centre, it crosses one synapse. A motor neuron carries it back down the leg. Then the effector, the thigh muscle, contracts.

scenes.tts: Zoom in on the motor neuron. Its dendrites receive signals, and the cell body gathers them. One long axon carries the signal away, in a large mammal sometimes a metre or more. Its terminals pass it on.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the ORANGE motor neuron as a cartoon: branching dendrites, round cell body with nucleus, a long axon wrapped in pale myelin segments with short bare gaps, branching terminals ending just above a RED muscle fibre, separated from it by a narrow visible gap. Each part is labelled as the narrator names it.
scenes.narration: Zoom in on the motor neuron. Its dendrites receive signals, and the cell body gathers them. One long axon carries the signal away, in a large mammal sometimes a metre or more. Its terminals pass it on.

scenes.tts: Along the axon the signal is an impulse. It is all or none: full size, or nothing at all. On many axons it hops between short bare gaps in a wrapping called myelin. At most synapses, the terminal releases a chemical that crosses a narrow gap.
scenes.visual: A bright ORANGE pulse runs along the axon, hopping gap to gap; a second, third and fourth pulse follow, each exactly the same height (small height ruler beside them, label 'all-or-none'). At the terminal, small dots spill across a narrow gap onto the muscle fibre (label 'chemical synapse').
scenes.narration: Along the axon the signal is an impulse. It is all or none: full size, or nothing at all. On many axons it hops between short bare gaps in a wrapping called myelin. At most synapses, the terminal releases a chemical that crosses a narrow gap.

scenes.tts: But how fast does the impulse run? In eighteen fifty, Hermann von Helmholtz asked that of a frog. He stimulated its nerve near the calf muscle and timed the twitch.
scenes.caption: But how fast does the impulse run? In 1850, Hermann von Helmholtz asked that of a frog. He stimulated its nerve near the calf muscle and timed the twitch.
scenes.visual: Cut to a cartoon frog calf muscle (RED) with its nerve (BLUE-ORANGE neutral line) running away from it. An electrode marked 'near' touches the nerve close to the muscle; a spark; the muscle twitches. Timer bar 1 fills: a short nerve segment, then a hatched GREY block 'junction + muscle'. On-screen: '1850'.
scenes.narration: But how fast does the impulse run? In 1850, Hermann von Helmholtz asked that of a frog. He stimulated its nerve near the calf muscle and timed the twitch.

scenes.tts: Then he moved the stimulus farther up the same nerve, and timed it again. Every time, the twitch came a little later than before.
scenes.visual: A second electrode marked 'far' touches the nerve farther from the muscle; a spark; a pulse travels the extra length; the muscle twitches. Timer bar 2 fills under bar 1: a longer nerve segment, then the same hatched GREY block. The two bars are stacked and left-aligned at the moment of the stimulus. Their hatched GREY blocks have the same width, but bar 2's block starts and ends later, leaving a visible gap between the bars' right ends.
scenes.narration: Then he moved the stimulus farther up the same nerve, and timed it again. Every time, the twitch came a little later than before.

scenes.tts: Each delay includes time at the junction and in the muscle. One part of these two delays belongs to the nerve alone. Which part?
scenes.visual: Both timer bars hold still. The hatched GREY blocks pulse gently. A question mark sits over the gap between the right ends of the two bars.
scenes.narration: Each delay includes time at the junction and in the muscle. One part of these two delays belongs to the nerve alone. Which part?

scenes.visual: Hold on the two stacked timer bars and the question mark; no motion except the slow pulse of the hatched blocks.

scenes.tts: The difference. The junction and the muscle take the same time in both trials, so they cancel. The extra delay belongs to the extra length of nerve.
scenes.visual: The hatched GREY blocks and the shared nerve length fade out of both bars. Only the extra piece of bar 2 remains, bright. A bracket on the nerve marks the extra length between the two electrodes; a dashed line links the bracket to the bright extra bar.
scenes.narration: The difference. The junction and the muscle take the same time in both trials, so they cancel. The extra delay belongs to the extra length of nerve.

scenes.tts: Divide that extra length by that extra time, and you get the nerve's own speed. Helmholtz found a few tens of metres per second, about a car on a motorway.
scenes.visual: On screen: 'v = difference in distance / difference in time'. Below it: 'frog nerve: a few tens of m per s'. A small car icon slides across the bottom of the frame at the same pace as a pulse travelling along the nerve.
scenes.narration: Divide that extra length by that extra time, and you get the nerve's own speed. Helmholtz found a few tens of metres per second, about a car on a motorway.

scenes.tts: Now back to the knee. Each axon's time is its length divided by its speed. In this model, each synapse in the cord adds about a millisecond. The junction and the muscle add a little more.
scenes.visual: Back to the leg and its GOLD route. The timer bar at the bottom fills as a pulse travels: a BLUE segment as the pulse climbs the sensory neuron (label 'length / speed'), a WHITE tick at the cord ('about 1 ms, model'), an ORANGE segment as it descends the motor neuron, then a small hatched GREY end block ('junction + muscle').
scenes.narration: Now back to the knee. Each axon's time is its length divided by its speed. In this model, each synapse in the cord adds about a millisecond. The junction and the muscle add a little more.

scenes.tts: The bar's legs add up to just under the measured time, when the thigh muscle's electrical signal starts. The bar leaves out the brief tap and stretch before the spindle fires. The kick itself comes later. Nearly all of the bar is time on the two axons.
scenes.visual: The full bar holds. A thin dashed sliver at the bar's start is labelled 'not drawn: tap to spindle firing (small)'. On-screen numbers (computed, model): 'sensory 8.3 ms', 'synapse 1 ms', 'motor 8.3 ms', 'junction + muscle about 1.5 ms', 'total about 19 ms', 'axons: about 87% of the model sum', and beside it 'measured: tap to muscle's electrical response, about 20 ms'. A small grey arrow beyond the bar's end reads 'visible kick: later'. The BLUE and ORANGE segments brighten; the tick and end block dim.
scenes.narration: The bar's legs add up to just under the measured time, when the thigh muscle's electrical signal starts. The bar leaves out the brief tap and stretch before the spindle fires. The kick itself comes later. Nearly all of the bar is time on the two axons.

scenes.tts: So a response is a route, and its time is the sum of its legs. Change a length, a speed, or the number of synapses, and the time changes.
scenes.visual: The five stations and the bar shrink to one diagram in the centre. Beneath it the equation writes itself: 'response time ≈ sum of L/v for each axon + synapses in the cord × about 1 ms + end delays', with a small tag 'simple model'. A slider nudges the BLUE segment longer and the whole bar lengthens with it.
scenes.narration: So a response is a route, and its time is the sum of its legs. Change a length, a speed, or the number of synapses, and the time changes.

scenes.visual: End card with the Hex mascot holding a stopwatch. Line: 'A response is a route; its time sums its legs.'
